content: The gag reflex is an involuntary protective mechanism designed to safeguard the pharynx and throat from foreign objects. It is a common issue during dental procedures, often making treatment distressing, challenging, or even impossible to perform. Various strategies have been proposed to manage the gag reflex, including pharmacological approaches (anti-nausea medications, sedatives, local and general anesthetics), non-pharmacological methods (herbal remedies, behavioral therapies, acupressure, acupuncture, laser therapy, and prosthetic devices), and combinations of these interventions. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of both pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions in managing gagging during dental treatment. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed interventions for patients experiencing gagging that interfered with dental procedures. Trials involving participants with central or peripheral nervous system disorders, oral lesions, systemic medications affecting gag reflex, or anatomical alterations due to surgery were excluded. Four trials with a total of 328 participants (263 adults and 65 children aged four years or older) were included. These trials primarily investigated acupuncture, acupressure, and laser therapy at the P6 point (a location on the inner forearm, three finger-breadths below the wrist, between two tendons). The outcomes measured included the successful completion of dental procedures and the reduction in gagging, as reported by both assessors and patients. 1. Acupuncture at P6: Acupuncture at P6 showed uncertain evidence for improving the successful completion of dental procedures (relative risk [RR] 1.78, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.05 to 3.01; two trials, 59 participants; very low-certainty evidence). It also showed uncertain evidence for reducing gagging (RR 2.57, 95% CI 1.12 to 5.89; one trial, 26 participants; very low-certainty evidence) compared to sham acupuncture. When combined with sedation, acupuncture at P6 did not demonstrate any significant difference compared to sham acupuncture with sedation (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.28; one trial, 34 participants; very low-certainty evidence). 2. Acupressure at P6: Thumb pressure acupressure, with or without sedation, showed no clear difference in completing dental procedures (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.10; one trial, 39 participants; very low-certainty evidence; and RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.46; one trial, 30 participants; very low-certainty evidence, respectively) or in reducing gagging (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.23; one trial, 39 participants; very low-certainty evidence; and RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.41; one trial, 30 participants; very low-certainty evidence) compared to sham acupressure. Acupressure using a device at P6 showed uncertain evidence for successful completion of dental procedures (RR 2.63, 95% CI 1.33 to 5.18; one trial, 34 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and for reducing gagging (RR 3.94, 95% CI 1.63 to 9.53; one trial, 34 participants; very low-certainty evidence) compared to sham acupressure. However, when combined with sedation, no significant differences were observed (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.48; one trial, 27 participants; very low-certainty evidence; and RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.69; one trial, 27 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Acupressure using a sea band, with or without sedation, showed no clear difference in completing dental procedures (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.17; one trial, 21 participants; very low-certainty evidence; and RR 1.80, 95% CI 0.63 to 5.16; one trial, 19 participants; very low-certainty evidence) or in reducing gagging (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.17; one trial, 21 participants; very low-certainty evidence; and RR 2.70, 95% CI 0.72 to 10.14; one trial, 19 participants; very low-certainty evidence) compared to sham acupressure. 3. Laser Therapy at P6: Laser therapy at P6 demonstrated a difference in the absence of gagging during dental procedures (odds ratio [OR] 86.33, 95% CI 29.41 to 253.45; one trial, 40 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and in reducing gagging (mean difference [MD] 1.80, 95% CI 1.53 to 2.07; one trial, 25 participants; very low-certainty evidence) compared to dummy laser application. No significant adverse effects were reported for any of the interventions. For acupuncture at P6, the trial authors were uncertain whether the reported adverse effects were due to participant anxiety or the intervention itself. None of the trials on acupressure or laser therapy reported on adverse effects. The evidence from these four trials was of very low certainty, making it insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of acupuncture, acupressure, or laser therapy at P6 in reducing gagging or facilitating the successful completion of dental procedures. No trials were identified that evaluated other interventions for managing the gag reflex during dental treatment. Further well-designed and well-reported trials are necessary to assess the efficacy of various interventions for this purpose.
